issues.legal_issue: A landlord may not forcibly dispossess a tenant who is in possession, even when the tenant’s rights are alleged to have ended because of unpaid land revenue.
material_facts: The tenants were cultivators in possession of the agricultural land.
The landlord allegedly prevented them from cultivating the land and caused others to cultivate it.
The landlord claimed that the tenants’ rights had been extinguished because land revenue was unpaid.
The statutory scheme allowed the revenue authority, in specified circumstances, to accept arrears and provided procedures for recovering arrears and ejecting a defaulter.
The landlord took possession without using the prescribed legal process.
issues.conclusion: The tenants’ alleged default did not entitle the landlord to take possession by force. The landlord had to proceed through the legally prescribed process, and the Board of Revenue’s decision was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 82(3) and 137 of the Qanoon Ryotwari, arrears could lead to extinguishment of a khatedar’s right, but the provision permitting acceptance of arrears in specified circumstances meant the right was not automatically extinguished in every case of arrears. The statutory recovery process could not be bypassed by forcible dispossession. Indian law does not permit a person to take forcible possession and requires possession to be obtained through a court or other lawful process: Midnapur Zamindary Company Limited v. Naresh Narayan Roy; K.K. Verma v. Naraindas C. Malkani; Yar Mohammad v. Lakshmi Das; and Wali Ahmad Khan v. Ayodhya Kundu.

rule.if: tenant_restoration_proceeding and tenant_in_possession and landlord_used_force_to_eject and recovery_process_not_used and (arrears_claimed or tenancy_rights_alleged_to_have_ended)

predicates.tenant_restoration_proceeding: A tenant brought a proceeding seeking restoration after being dispossessed.
predicates.tenant_in_possession: The tenant was in possession of the land before the disputed dispossession.
predicates.landlord_used_force_to_eject: The landlord used force or self-help to remove the tenant from possession.
predicates.recovery_process_not_used: The landlord took possession without first using the legally prescribed recovery process.
predicates.arrears_claimed: The landlord relied on the tenant’s failure to pay land revenue as a basis for taking possession.
predicates.tenancy_rights_alleged_to_have_ended: The landlord alleged that the tenant’s rights had ended.

issues.definition: When a tenant seeking restoration was in possession and the landlord used force without the prescribed recovery process, the landlord must obtain possession through lawful process, including when arrears or ended tenancy rights are relied on.

issues.legal_issue: A summary possessory suit for unlawful dispossession concerns prior possession rather than title, and forcible entry by a landlord may constitute trespass for that purpose.
material_facts: The cultivators sought restoration of agricultural land under the summary procedure for unlawful disturbance of possession.
They alleged that they had been in possession and were forcibly prevented from cultivating the land.
The landlord argued that entry onto the land was not trespass because the cultivators’ tenancy had ended.
The statutory scheme provided a summary procedure for restoration after unlawful disturbance and a separate, longer procedure for other possession claims.
issues.conclusion: The summary possessory provision applied to forcible dispossession by a landlord. The alleged title or termination of the tenants’ rights was irrelevant to that proceeding, which turns on possession and dispossession otherwise than in due course of law.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 163 of the Qanoon Ryotwari and 326 of the Qanoon Mal provide for suits concerning trespass and obstruction, including summary restoration where possession has been unlawfully disturbed. Section 326 is similar in structure to section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877; “disturbed unlawfully” means disturbed otherwise than in due course of law, and “trespass” includes forcible entry and dispossession by a landlord. Title is irrelevant in such a possessory proceeding. The Court relied on the principles in Midnapur Zamindary Company Limited v. Naresh Narayan Roy, K.K. Verma v. Naraindas C. Malkani, Yar Mohammad v. Lakshmi Das, and Wali Ahmad Khan v. Ayodhya Kundu.

predicates.summary_possessory_proceeding: A person sought summary restoration of possession under a procedure for unlawful disturbance of possession.
predicates.prior_possession: The claimant was in possession before the disputed dispossession.
predicates.dispossession_not_in_due_course_of_law: The claimant was removed from possession otherwise than through lawful process.

issues.definition: When a person seeks summary restoration after being dispossessed otherwise than through lawful process, and had prior possession, restoration may be decided without inquiring into title.
